title: Space
ks3: Space physics: the Solar System, day and night, seasons, gravity and light years
intro: The Sun, the planets and beyond. Practise day and night, years and seasons, the Moon, gravity on other worlds and light years.
description: Free KS3 Physics space questions with answers: the Solar System, day and night, seasons, the Moon, gravity and weight on other planets, stars, galaxies and light years. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: Why do we have day and night?
options: The Earth spins on its axis
The Sun moves round the Earth
The Moon blocks the Sun at night
questions.hint: Which way is your side of the Earth facing?
questions.explain: The Earth spins. The side facing the Sun has day, and the side facing away has night.

questions.q: How long does the Earth take to travel once round the Sun?
questions.hint: Think of birthdays.
questions.explain: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun once. That is one year. (The extra quarter days make a leap year every four years.)

questions.q: How long does the Earth take to spin round once?
questions.hint: One spin gives one day and one night.
questions.explain: The Earth spins once about every 24 hours, giving one day and one night.

questions.q: Why does the UK have summer and winter?
options: The Earth is much closer to the Sun in summer
The Sun gets hotter in summer
The Moon blocks the Sun in winter
questions.hint: It isn't about distance: the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in January.
questions.explain: The Earth's axis is tilted. When the UK is tilted towards the Sun, the days are longer and the Sun is higher in the sky, so it is summer.

questions.q: In the UK, in which direction does the Sun rise in the morning?
questions.hint: The Sun rises in the east and…
questions.explain: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. It only looks as if the Sun moves: really the Earth is spinning.

questions.q: When it is summer in the UK, what season is it in Australia?
questions.hint: Australia is in the other half (hemisphere) of the Earth.
questions.explain: When the northern half of the Earth is tilted towards the Sun (UK summer), the southern half is tilted away, so Australia has winter.

questions.q: What is at the centre of our Solar System?
questions.hint: All the planets orbit it.
questions.explain: The Sun is at the centre. The Earth and the other planets orbit it.

questions.q: Which of these is a star?
questions.hint: A star makes its own light.
questions.explain: The Sun is our nearest star. The Moon is a moon, and Mars and the Earth are planets.

questions.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
questions.hint: The order starts: M, V, E, M…
questions.explain: The order from the Sun is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

questions.q: Why can we see the Moon?
options: It reflects light from the Sun
It glows because it is hot
questions.hint: Is the Moon a light source?
questions.explain: The Moon doesn't make its own light. We see it because it reflects sunlight.

questions.q: About how long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth once?
questions.hint: The word "month" comes from "moon".
questions.explain: The Moon takes about 27 days to orbit the Earth. From one full moon to the next is about 29½ days.

questions.q: Which is the largest planet in our Solar System?
questions.hint: It is a giant made mostly of gas.
questions.explain: Jupiter is the largest planet. More than 1000 Earths could fit inside it.

questions.q: Why does the Moon seem to change shape over a month (its phases)?
options: As it orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half
The Earth's shadow covers part of it
questions.hint: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun.
questions.explain: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see more or less of that lit half, from new moon to full moon and back.

questions.q: What happens in a solar eclipse?
options: The Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks the sunlight
The Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon
The Sun stops shining for a while
questions.hint: Something gets in the way of the Sun.
questions.explain: In a solar eclipse, the Moon moves between the Sun and the Earth, so its shadow falls on part of the Earth. Never look straight at the Sun, even during an eclipse.

questions.q: Jupiter's gravitational field strength is about 25 N/kg. What would a 2 kg bag weigh on Jupiter?
questions.hint: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
questions.explain: 2 kg × 25 N/kg = 50 N. On Earth the same bag weighs only 20 N.

questions.q: Why does an astronaut weigh less on the Moon than on the Earth?
options: The Moon has less mass, so its gravity is weaker
There is no air on the Moon
The Moon is further from the Sun
questions.hint: Gravity depends on how much mass a planet or moon has.
questions.explain: The Moon has much less mass than the Earth, so its gravitational field is weaker. The astronaut's mass stays the same, but their weight is less.

questions.q: Which force keeps the Earth in orbit around the Sun?
questions.hint: It is the same force that keeps the Moon going round the Earth.
questions.explain: The Sun's gravity pulls on the Earth and keeps it moving in its orbit.

questions.q: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon?
questions.hint: Mass is the amount of stuff in you. Does going to the Moon change that?
questions.explain: Mass does not change from place to place, so it is still 70 kg. Only her weight changes, because the Moon's gravity is weaker.

questions.q: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg. What is his weight on the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is 1.6 N/kg?
questions.hint: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
questions.explain: W = m × g = 80 kg × 1.6 N/kg = 128 N. On Earth he would weigh 80 × 10 = 800 N.

questions.q: A Moon rover weighs 1600 N on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). What does it weigh on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg)?
questions.hint: Find the rover's mass first.
questions.explain: Mass = W ÷ g = 1600 N ÷ 10 N/kg = 160 kg. On the Moon, W = 160 kg × 1.6 N/kg = 256 N.

questions.q: Astronauts float around inside the International Space Station, about 400 km above the Earth. Is there gravity there?
options: Yes, but they float because they and the station are falling round the Earth together
No, there is no gravity in space
No, because there is no air in space
Yes, but it pushes them upwards
questions.hint: What keeps the space station going round the Earth?
questions.explain: The Earth's gravity is still strong there, only a little weaker than on the ground. It keeps the station in orbit. The station and the astronauts fall round the Earth together, so they float.

questions.q: What is a light year?
options: The distance light travels in one year
The time light takes to travel one year
A year on a different planet
questions.hint: It sounds like a time, but it isn't.
questions.explain: A light year is a distance: how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 million million km. It is used for distances to stars.

questions.q: What is the name of the galaxy that our Solar System is in?
questions.hint: On a very dark night you can see it as a milky band across the sky.
questions.explain: We live in the Milky Way galaxy, which has hundreds of billions of stars. Andromeda is a different galaxy nearby.

questions.q: What are the stars that we see in the night sky?
options: Suns like ours, but very far away
questions.hint: Our Sun is a star too.
questions.explain: Stars are huge, hot balls of gas that make their own light, like our Sun. They look tiny because they are so far away.

questions.q: Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth. If the Sun suddenly stopped shining, when would we notice?
questions.hint: The last light to leave the Sun is still on its way to us.
questions.explain: Light already on its way would keep arriving for about 8 minutes, so we would not notice until then.

questions.q: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, is about 4.2 light years away. How many years does its light take to reach us?
questions.hint: A light year is the distance light travels in one year.
questions.explain: Each light year takes light one year to cross, so 4.2 light years take 4.2 years. The light we see tonight left the star over 4 years ago.
